IBNKATHIR, d. 774 (author): In the divine hadith, “prayer” means recitation, as in 17:110; because the Fatiha details the division, its recitation is a major pillar of prayer. | mentions 17:110 BURHAN, d. 794 (ابن حبان): Ibn Hibban reads the report comparing al-Fatiha with the Torah and Gospel as a difference in reward granted by God’s favor, not as intrinsic superiority within the Quran. BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 (author): The Fatiha's purpose is to establish God's exclusive right to all praise and perfection, sovereignty over both worlds, worship and aid, and to ask for the path of the successful rather than the doomed; its center is مراقبة. BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 (الحرالي): The basmala relates to the Fatiha as the Fatiha relates to the Qur'an: each is a compact synthesis of what the larger whole details. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): A sacred hadith says al-Fatiha is divided equally between God and servant, with the servant entitled to what is asked; its opening praises and glorifies God, its middle is shared, and its ending is the servant's supplication. ng praise prepares the request for guidance.", "reasons": "RAZI, d. 606 (author): Razi sketches the sūra’s sequence: seek refuge from sins, begin good works in God’s name, praise and recognize his lordship and mercy, heed judgment, worship and seek help, ask guidance, and avoid ignorance and error. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): The seven Fatiha verses remove seven vices: praise dispels desire, Lord of the worlds greed, Judgment Day anger, worship and aid pride and vanity, guidance caprice, the favored path unbelief and doubt, and the final phrase innovation. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (الله تعالى): In a divine report transmitted by the Prophet, God responds to each Fatiha phrase: the opening remembers Him, praise praises Him, the mercy names magnify Him, Judgment Day glorifies Him or is entrusted to Him, worship belongs to Him, aid relies on Him, and guidance is the servant's request. NASAFI, d. 710 (أبو هريرة عن النبي): Abu Hurayra reports God’s dialogue dividing the Fatiha between Himself and the servant: praise, glorification, and exaltation belong to God; the worshipper’s request for guidance and the response to it belong to the servant, while worship and aid are shared. BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 (الحرالي): Al-Harali contrasts the Qur'an's detailed, dispersed sequence with the Fatiha's seven complete universals, and makes the Fatiha a mirror of the servant's move from misguidance to guidance. | mentions 93:7 ITQAN, d. 911 (الإمام فخر الدين): Fakhr al-Din maps the Qur’an’s four aims—God, resurrection, prophethood, and divine decree—onto the Fatiha: praise, Judgment Day, worship and reliance, and guidance through the surah’s end; this supports its name Umm al-Qur’an. | mentions 1:2, 1:4, 1:6, 1:7 ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): The basmala is the crown, the Qur’an a perfect body, Fatiha its head, and alhamdu lillah its face; mercy, guidance, worship, and divine unity express its spiritual life. QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 (author): The short surah gathers core Islamic creed, worldview, feelings, and guidance, explaining its repetition in every rakʿa and why prayer without it is invalid. QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 (رسول الله): Abu Hurayra reports in Sahih Muslim that God calls al-Fatiha a prayer divided between Himself and His servant: praise, mercy, and glorification are the Lord's; worship and aid are shared; guidance and the servant's request belong to the servant, who receives what he asks. ABUDAWUD (الله تعالى): In a hadith qudsi transmitted by Abu Hurayra, God divides al-Fatiha between Himself and the servant: praise and glorification receive divine responses, worship is mutual, and the guidance petition belongs to the servant. {"id": "2:31/q05", "question": "Which names did Adam learn?", "turns_on": "The scope of 'all' and whether the masculine display pronoun narrows the named beings.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q05/p1", "position": "The names of every created thing, great and small, in all kinds and times.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatāda and many others mention ordinary vessels, animals, landforms and even bodily terms. Al-Jishumī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr and al-Ālūsī favor breadth from 'all'; the intercession report has Adam taught every name. Reports vary on inclusion of future beings and crafts. Ibn Isḥāq says Adam named every thing, and that each name remains attached to its thing until the Resurrection."}, {"id": "2:31/q05/p2", "position": "Only the names of the angels.", "reasons": "Attributed to al-Rabīʿ and other early transmitters; the reports vary in his exact identity."}, {"id": "2:31/q05/p3", "position": "Only the names of Adam's descendants.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd says the descendants were taken from Adam's back and displayed; Elmalılı notes the pronoun's rational plural and suggests seedlike or intellectual forms."}, {"id": "2:31/q05/p4", "position": "Names of the creatures and things of earth, especially animals and birds.", "reasons": "Muqātil individually names horse, mule, donkey; Ibn Qutayba and al-Kalbī limit scope to earth. Ibn ʿĀshūr restricts initial vocabulary to concrete things needed in humanity's first world."}, {"id": "2:31/q05/p5", "position": "Names of Adam's descendants and the angels together.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī prefers this because ʿaraḍahum ordinarily denotes rational persons. Later authors transmit his view; al-Rabīʿ is also reported with this combination."}, {"id": "2:31/q05/p6", "position": "God's own names, or a hidden divine name by which Adam learned all names.", "reasons": "Al-Jurayrī speaks of a hidden name; al-Ḥakīm al-Tirmidhī of divine names. Al-Qushayrī and Bursevī include both divine and creaturely names, arguing that divine names imply still greater honor."}, {"id": "2:31/q05/p7", "position": "The making of every kind of thing, including crafts.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī and al-Baghawī report the narrower craft explanation. Jishumī, Ṭabrisī and later authors include tools, cultivation, medicine, mining and life-sustaining skills within the broad reading."}, {"id": "2:31/q05/p8", "position": "Only stars' names.", "reasons": "Reported from Ḥumayd al-Shāmī; Abū Ḥayyān also reports an attribution to Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and Qatāda."}, {"id": "2:31/q05/p9", "position": "Names of broad kinds rather than each individual or later subtype.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima gives human, angel, jinn and bird; another report names mountains, horses and valleys, with later descendants assigning other labels. Al-Zajjāj's linguists call them genera."}, {"id": "2:31/q05/p10", "position": "A word or power of naming that unlocks every name.", "reasons": "Al-Naqqāsh reports one word from Ibn ʿAbbās; Abū Ḥayyān reports the majority's act-of-naming reading; Kur'an Yolu describes a capacity to invent language."}, {"id": "2:31/q05/p11", "position": "The hidden living realities preserved with God, of which worldly names are descended signs.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī argues from the living plural referents and 15:21's imperishable treasuries; their plurality is of ranks, not separate individuals. Verbal labels cannot account for Adam's distinction over angels."}, {"id": "2:31/q05/p12", "position": "Adam was taught everything, even advanced grammar such as Sībawayh's.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī is reported with this extreme claim; Ibn ʿAṭiyya explicitly calls it wrong on several grounds."}]}
{"id": "2:31/q23", "question": "Why did God ask angels to give the names?", "turns_on": "Exposing ignorance, displaying Adam's merit, demonstrating fitness for rule, or an impossible command.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q23/p1", "position": "The challenge exposes the angels' ignorance of what is before them and of the unseen future.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash says no prior claim is needed; al-Wāḥidī compares 2:23. The inability rebukes conjecture about corruption; many sources stress God already knew they could not answer. Al-Ṭabarī's possible reconstruction makes the challenge test an inference that exceeded what God had disclosed: the angels generalized from some corrupt descendants to all, while many obedient reformers were hidden from them. Al-Ḥasan, Qatāda and al-Rabīʿ instead report that the challenge exposed a private boast about angelic knowledge and honor."}, {"id": "2:31/q23/p2", "position": "It is a teaching prompt contingent on whether the angels know; no obligation to do the impossible was imposed.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī reports al-Akhfash, al-Jubbāʾī and ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā; Ibn ʿAṭiyya's discerning exegetes and many later authors reject an impossible-duty inference."}, {"id": "2:31/q23/p3", "position": "The question demonstrates Adam's knowledge and superior fitness for vicegerency.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī says governance and justice require knowledge of capacities and rights; al-Ṭabrisī names crafts, farming and finding resources; Ibn ʿĀshūr stresses analysis and guidance, whereas angels execute fixed tasks. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the demonstrated distinction supplies detailed evidence that Adam is fit to be steward. Al-Rabīʿ reports that God taught Adam the names to show his superiority over angels who had privately boasted of superior knowledge and honor."}, {"id": "2:31/q23/p4", "position": "It is a permissible incapacitating command even though God knew the angels could not comply.", "reasons": "Some infer that God may command the impossible; Bursevī likens this to commanding image makers to animate their images at Judgment Day."}, {"id": "2:31/q23/p5", "position": "It invites the angels to learn by direct test, observation and reflection.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu contrasts a reported explanation with demonstrated certainty; the test gives the angels a higher certainty and recognition of Adam's capacities."}]}
{"id": "2:31/q26", "question": "What claim is ‘if you are truthful’ testing?", "turns_on": "Sources connect it to several distinct prior or implied angelic claims, or simply to accuracy in naming.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q26/p1", "position": "Their assumption that God would create none more knowledgeable, honored or excellent than themselves.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda's accounts say they privately boasted of prior worship and precedence; Adam's lesson and their admission correct the assumption. Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda report that the angels' boast was private; al-Rabīʿ says the episode exposed both their public words and their hidden claim of superior knowledge and honor."}, {"id": "2:31/q26/p2", "position": "Their forecast that the earthly successor would corrupt and shed blood.", "reasons": "Reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd and Companions connect it to 2:30; inability to know visible names exposes uncertainty about future unseen conduct. Al-Ṭabarī suspects a transmitter's error and reconstructs the report: the angels inferred that all descendants would corrupt from a statement concerning some, though God concealed the many who would obey, reform the earth and preserve blood. He expressly says this explains a possible report, not his chosen interpretation of the verse. He rejects the version in which God had already informed the angels of corruption and then reproached them for repeating it."}, {"id": "2:31/q26/p3", "position": "Their implicit claim that they deserved vicegerency because of purity, worship or sinlessness.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī mentions their own glorification against another creature's disobedience; al-Bayḍāwī and Asad take purity as the implied claim, and Elmalılı makes governance the test."}, {"id": "2:31/q26/p4", "position": "Their ability to give a correct answer about the names, without a specific earlier boast.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash calls it exposure of ignorance; al-Naqqāsh says the accuracy condition excludes speculative ijtihād, comparing the mistaken guess in 2:259. Abū Ḥayyān says truthful means correct rather than merely non-lying."}, {"id": "2:31/q26/p5", "position": "Their implied judgment that appointing Adam was unfitting for God's wisdom.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī allows truthfulness of an implication in a question; Ibn ʿĀshūr considers whether the angels' words were an objection or a submissive request for explanation."}]}
{"id": "2:31/q27", "question": "What does Adam's lesson show about knowledge and its possessors?", "turns_on": "How the lesson establishes Adam's rank and the value of knowledge relative to worship, authority, and mere labels.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q27/p1", "position": "Divinely taught knowledge gives Adam public honor, priority over angels and fitness for vicegerency.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī contrasts secret teaching with public display; al-Baghawī uses it for prophetic rank over angels. Al-Rāzī argues knowledge, rather than strength or wealth, explains prostration and leadership. Ibn ʿĀshūr connects naming to practical analysis, justice and human governance. Ibn ʿĀshūr links Adam's demonstrated distinction to his fitness as steward and to what the angels did not know. Al-Rabīʿ says Adam's taught names showed his superiority after angels had privately claimed that no creature would exceed their knowledge or honor."}, {"id": "2:31/q27/p2", "position": "Knowledge is more exalted than uncomprehending worship and demands humility, practice and fear of God.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī contrasts angelic praise with knowing; al-Rāzī adduces 35:28, 39:9, 58:11, 96:1-5, 20:114 and many reports, distinctions among kinds of scholars, and warnings about hoarding, vanity and knowledge without action. Bursevī traces knowledge to love and obedience."}]}
